extracted.intended_audience: natural philosophers, scientific readers, naturalists, and practical craftsmen (tanners, instrument-makers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for preparing and reporting observational natural-history and practical-technology accounts (astronomical observations, biological tables, and tanning machinery/processes) including what to record, how to illustrate, and how to specify apparatus. Emphasis on precise observations, figures/tables, material preparation, and machine dimensions/operation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comet observation reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Record precise observational details: date and local hour, point of first sighting above horizon and bearing (e.g. from west to east-south-east), initial apparent bulk and brightness, evolution over successive dates (change in brightness and bulk), location relative to known stars and constellations, measured tail length (e.g. about 23 degrees), orientation of tail relative to sun, and colour/visual effects (reflections on sea/shore). Note whether the globe/head is distinguishable by naked eye or requires a telescope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Father Estancel (St. Salvador, 5 Mar 1668 NST at 7 o'clock) observed the comet 'a little above the horizon... appeared in its greatest bulk... whole length being about 23 degrees'; the tail was always directly opposite to the sun; early brightness lasted about three days then decreased though bulk continued to increase. Record also when fixed stars are seen through the chevelure and the passage through constellations. Where relevant, note instrument use (telescope) and when naked-eye visibility suffices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice and preparation of tanning materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Use every part of the oak-tree or oaken coppice wood (of any age/size) cut and procured in 'barking time'; dry the material very well in the sun and more so than bark; house and keep dry until use; shave, cleft, bruise or cut larger wood to sizes fit for the engine; kiln-dry and then grind as tanners usually do their bark.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If oak is scarce, thorns may substitute; birch, when prepared and used instead of oak, is suitable for sole-leather. Proper season and thorough drying are emphasised to avoid spoilage and blackening of hides. Using these materials (properly prepared) can tan as well as bark alone and at lower cost, conserving timber and improving value of underwoods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drying timing to avoid spoilage in tanning
rubrics_metrics.description: Materials intended for immediate use require more thorough kiln-drying than material stored for later use; insufficient drying will cause blackening and spoil the leather.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit warning: 'Such wood as is to be used presently after getting it, will require the more drying on the kiln; otherwise it will blacken and spoil all the leather.' Plan drying schedule accordingly based on intended use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine construction specifications for beating and cutting tanning materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct a long square wooden block (oak or elm recommended) with specified dimensions (length ~4 feet; breadth ~3–16 inches as given; depth 8–10 inches) and add iron fittings: a square cavity to receive an iron plate anvil (about 4 inches deep, 9 inches broad, 12 inches long), iron clasping piece across the middle (~3 inches broad) with hooks and hinge loops, and additional iron plates/grooves to guide and hold the cutting knife.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design features include hooks to hang a weight during bruising/cutting, a button to lift the clasping piece, places for four feet at appropriate working height, and provision for fitting and unscrewing knife ends so the knife can be slipped out and stored. Follow the illustrated plate figures (pl. 6, figs. 4–6) for relative placement of parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine operation and tool dimensions
rubrics_metrics.description: Specify hammer and knife sizes and finishes: hammer for beating/bruising ~6 lb with ~3 in square head for two-handed use, or ~3 lb with ~2 in square head for one-handed/youth use; one end of hammer smooth, the other dented; handles ~1 foot long (longer for larger hammer). Knife to cut bruised stuff ~8 inches broad and nearly as deep, made like a tobacco-knife with handle; knife guided by iron plates in grooves and fastened by screw-pins and removable fittings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure hammers are well steeled at both ends. Knife should run in grooves and be removable for storage and maintenance. Provide two long square iron plates at the cutting end with the nearer plate slightly lower and the block pared for efficient falling-off of cut material. Hollow the block under the cutting hole and slope the end so cut material falls away as it is cut.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clasping, weighting, and feeding operation details
rubrics_metrics.description: Include a clasping iron across the engine to hold material while bruising/cutting with upward turned hooks (to engage hinges) and a single hook on the other side for hanging a weight; use left hand to furnish the knife with bruised materials while right hand cuts; provide a button to raise the clasping piece for insertion of materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weight should be hung appropriately during bruising or cutting to hold material steady. Configure the hollow cutting cavity 'as near as may be' but large enough for the knife to fall and rise freely, and shape surfaces for efficient hand-work coordination (left hand feeding, right hand cutting).

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparing and presenting malacological tables and figures
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare tables of shells with lively figures (illustrations) of each shell, reserve sea-shells and rock-stones for later parts, and consult and include other authors for sea-shells if possible; number and explain figures by tables; omit figures (e.g., naked snails) in specimens when not material to the part of the design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to give the reader an exact view of animal-shells as well as fossils figured like shells so they can judge origins. Use comparative views to clarify arguments about origins and include plate numbers and figure references for reader navigation (see 'Table of English Snails... See Plate vi.').

rubrics_metrics.name: Research questions / agenda for land and freshwater snail studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Pose explicit queries to guide investigation: (1) whether other shell-snails exist on land beyond turbinate forms; (2) whether the insects are truly androgynous and both deposit eggs; (3) whether Roman methods of fattening (paved places encircled with water) are useful to observe generation; (4) what anatomy reveals about other taxa; (5) whether black spots on horns are eyes or antennae equivalents; (6) whether coccinea sanguis is saliva rather than extravasated blood; (7) in which snails stones ('bezoar-like') are found and their timing/medicinal virtues; (8) medicinal virtues of snails (restorative uses); (9) mechanical uses of snail saliva (dyeing, whitening wax/hair).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author provides tentative answers to some (e.g., 1 'Probably not'; 2 each individual appears truly androgynous; 5 'Uncertain'; 8 snails considered restorative). Use these queries to structure observational sampling, anatomy dissections, seasonal collection, and experimental trials (e.g., fattening enclosures) and record explicit evidence for/against each query.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxonomic table formatting and classification conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Organise species into clear categories (terrestres, terrestres nudae/limaces, fluviatiles, buccina, compressa testa, bivalvae, marine, etc.), provide latinized names and vernacular/local locality notes, and number entries with plate/figure cross-references (e.g., N° I–V, Plate vi).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include brief morphological descriptors (e.g., operculum type, spiral counts, color, habitats) and locality data (e.g., 'agri Hartfordiensis', 'agri Lincolniensis') so readers can cross-identify specimens and compare across regions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting anomalous medical/anecdotal observations (corroboration and citation)
rubrics_metrics.description: When presenting surprising medical/anecdotal cases (e.g., aged woman giving suck), support the account with corroboration by credible persons and cross-reference authoritative sources (e.g., Diemerbroeck's Anatome corporis humani) and include at least one additional recorded instance where possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phrase such relations as reportable if confirmable by 'very credible persons' and give references for further authority. Use multiple attestations or literature citations to strengthen acceptance of unusual physiological claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for reviewing scientific treatises
rubrics_metrics.description: Summarise and evaluate the treatise components (structure and chapter topics), relate its claims to prior experimental work (e.g., Boylean experiments), state where the author's hypotheses differ from contemporaries, and discuss what experiments or demonstrations the work relies on or suggests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a balanced account of the author's positions (e.g., nitro-aerial spirit/oxygen theory antecedents), note where experiments support or undermine claims, and compare to contemporary theories (Descartes, Boyle). Suggest experiments where the author does, and indicate how the work advances or contrasts with current mechanical/chemical theories.
